12115-discoveries-in-australia-volume-1-:
Commander J. Lort Stokes published this first volume in 1846, reporting the early years of HMS Beagle survey of Australian coasts, 1837 to 1843. Stokes, who served under Captain Robert FitzRoy, dedicated the work to his old shipmate.

The volume follows the Beagle from Plymouth to Bahia, from the Cape to Swan River, and along the north-west coast to Roebuck Bay and the Fitzroy River. Stokes describes harbors, reefs, and rivers, with notes on birds, plants, and Aboriginal people met along the way. Captain Owen Stanley visits to the Arafura Sea islands close the book. As a survey narrative, it pairs navigation detail with the wonder of coasts no European chart had yet fixed.
12411-the-long-white-cloud-ao-tea-roa:
William Pember Reeves, Agent-General in London for New Zealand, published this 1899 history under its Maori name, Ao Tea Roa, the Long White Cloud. Photographs and drawings illustrate the text, and Reeves thanks Major-General Robley for a tail-piece showing the Maori moko, or face tattoo, in minute and correct pattern.

The history moves from Maori settlement and custom through European contact, conflict and the building of a colony. Reeves writes as both administrator and storyteller, fond of his subject and clear about its peoples. The volume remains a readable, illustrated introduction to New Zealand's past, written by a man who helped govern its present.
16035-the-food-of-the-gods-a-popular-acc:
A popular account of cocoa by Brandon Head, issued in London by R. Brimley Johnson in 1903. Head takes his title from the Greek Theobroma, food of the gods. A colour plate shows East Indian coolies on a Trinidad cacao estate. The book explains a familiar food from tree to cup, for general readers.

Chapters treat cocoa's nature, its growth and cultivation, and its manufacture into chocolate and drink. Head follows the bean from tropical farms to London shops. His prose stays clear and enthusiastic, with pictures to help. The book still pleases food readers: a small luxury, traced to its roots in sun, soil, and labour.
28385-the-hunter-cats-of-connorloa:
Helen Jackson, writing as H. H., published The Hunter Cats of Connorloa in Boston in 1886, as part of her Cat Stories. A note in this e-text states that only The Hunter Cats of Connorloa is transcribed here, not the companion stories Letters from a Cat and Mammy Tittleback and Her Family.

The story opens with Mr. Connor, a sick and lonely traveller who has wandered the world seeking a climate that would restore his health. At last he settles in California, builds a house, and gathers his books and comforts about him. The cats of Connorloa, hunters by nature, become the lively centre of his new home life.
31574-a-new-subspecies-of-slider-turtle-:
John M. Legler's A New Subspecies of Slider Turtle, Pseudemys scripta, from Coahuila, México, was published as University of Kansas Publications, volume thirteen, number three, pages 73 to 84, on August 16, 1960. Legler, writing for the University of Kansas at Lawrence, names and describes a slider turtle from Coahuila, distinguishing it from its relatives by shell, pattern, and measurements.

The paper, printed at Topeka by the state printer, follows the standard form of taxonomic description: diagnosis, description, comparison, and range. For herpetologists, it fixes a new name for a Mexican population of a widespread turtle. Readers of natural history will find a precise, illustrated piece of species work, grounded in specimens from northern Mexico.
31862-the-story-of-sitka-the-historic-ou:
C. L. Andrews's Story of Sitka, published at Seattle, tells the historic outpost of the northwest coast and chief factory of the Russian American Company. Around a hundred years back, Sitka stood as the northwest coast's trading and civilized hub, welcoming Kronstadt vessels, China-bound New England clippers, and English traders and explorers.

Nine chapters cover discovery, settlement, progress of the colony, natives, churches and schools, social life, trade and industry, Sitka under United States rule, and what to see. Readers get a compact local history, illustrated with views of Mount Edgecumbe, the cathedral of St. Michael, and Baranof Castle.
536-a-footnote-to-history-eight-years-of:
Robert Louis Stevenson recounts eight years of strife in Samoa in this contemporary history, written from Vailima. Rival kings, German, British, and American consuls, and island chiefs tangle in wars, treaties, and betrayals. Stevenson, who knew the actors himself, owns his errors and his partial temper with frank candor.

Chapters treat native discord, foreign meddling, and the slow path to a settlement. Samoan words keep their nasal ng in his spelling. The book stands as a vivid, partisan footnote by a writer turned island witness, keen on justice for a small land caught between empires.
a-footnote-to-history-eight-years-of-tro:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this work of history about the struggle for Samoa. He lived at Vailima, on the island of Upolu. His preface admits the affair might rate only a few lines in a general history. Yet he expands it to a volume. The country was distracted, he says, and the truth was hard to come by among clashing rumors. Most of the actors were his own acquaintance. That made plain speaking delicate.

The tale begins with the seeds of discord among Samoan chiefs. It follows eight years of civil war. Foreign consuls and warships crowd the scene. Rival kings draw backing from Germany, Britain, and the United States. Stevenson writes as a friend of the Samoans and a critic of the powers. The book is his one long work of political reporting.
britannica-1911-actinozoa:
Actinozoa is a term in systematic zoology. Blainville coined it about 1834. It designated animals built radially about a centre. His group mixed very unlike creatures together. Single-celled forms stood beside sea-anemones and corals. Jelly-fish, hydroid polyps, and echinoderms were included. Polyzoa and rotifers crowded in as well. Huxley later restricted the term sharply.

Anatomy gave Huxley his dividing line. True coelenterates are built of two cell layers. Those layers match the first two in vertebrate development. Within them, Actinozoa release their embryos from inside. The young escape generally by the mouth. Sea-anemones, corals, and sea-pens form the group. The comb jellies stand on its other side. Later work kept Huxley's scheme with small changes.
britannica-1911-batticaloa:
Batticaloa is the capital of the eastern province of Ceylon, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the east coast of the island, sixty-nine miles south-south-east of Trincomalee, set on an island in a great lagoon. The town held 9969 people in 1901; its district, of 2872 square miles, held 143,161. The town matters for its haven and for the salt lagoons next to it.

Work and wonders close the account. An old Dutch fort of 1682 still stands in the town, which is the seat of a government agent and a district judge. Rice and coconuts are the district's two staples, and steamers trading round the island call at the port. The lagoon is famed for its “singing fish,” thought to be shell-fish that give out musical notes from the water. A remnant of Veddahs, the wild men of the woods, is also noted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-de-ul:
Antoine de Ulloa, a Spanish naval officer and scientist born at Seville in 1716, joined a French expedition to measure the earth in Peru. With Jorge Juan he spent nearly ten years at the equator, measuring a degree of the meridian. On the voyage home the British captured his ship, and his learning won him release and a fellowship of the Royal Society.

Later he governed Louisiana for two years and rose to lieutenant-general of the navy. He founded Spain's first museum of natural history and wrote on South America, its peoples, and its nature. With Juan he also wrote a secret report on Spanish America, published long after his death, that exposed early colonial rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-bur:
Francisco Burgoa, born at Oaxaca about 1600 and dead at Teopozotlan in 1681, was a Dominican historian of his native Mexican state. He entered the order on 2 August 1629, soon became master in theology, served as curate of several Indian parishes, and knew the Zapotec and Mixtec languages thoroughly. In 1649 he became provincial of San Hipolito province and attended his order's general chapter at Rome in 1656. He returned with titles as vicar-general, member of the Spanish Inquisition, and commissary and inspector of libraries in New Spain.

 His two great works are the Palestra historica, a history of the Dominican province of Oaxaca published at Mexico in 1670, and a geographical description of northern America published in 1674. They are voluminous and very rare, valuable though not absolutely reliable on every topic, and he also left sermons and a manuscript itinerary from Oaxaca to Rome and back.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-de-:
Francisco de Figueroa, surnamed the Divine, was a celebrated Spanish poet born at Alcala de Henares about 1540 and dead there in 1620. An editor's note gives the more probable dates 1530 to 1588. Of noble family and educated at Alcala University, he followed a military career for a time, campaigning in Italy and Flanders. From a very young age he showed unusual poetic talent, his poems full of fire and passion.

Following Boscan and Garcilaso, he wrote pastoral poems in Italian metres. He was among the first Spanish poets to use blank verse with success, a form Boscan had introduced in 1543. His best-known work is the eclogue Tirsis, written wholly in blank verse, and Cervantes praised him highly in Galatea. Sadly, most of his poems were burned by his own order before his death, and only a small part, published at Lisbon in 1625, survives.

Francisco de Ulloa was a Spanish explorer of California whose life and death remain uncertain, a figure known through conflicting histories. No one knows when he came to Mexico or whether he sailed with Cortes on his first California expedition. Diaz del Castillo tells that, during Cortes's absence, his wife sent letters by Ulloa begging his return. Ulloa, with two ships of provisions, reached Cortes when he was sorely pressed, returning to Mexico in 1537.

Eager for discovery, Cortes fitted out a fleet at his own expense in 1538 and sent three boats under Ulloa. Clavigero says Ulloa sailed along the California peninsula until shortage of provisions forced him back to New Spain, where in 1540, according to Diaz, a soldier stabbed and killed him. Other historians say his ship Trinidad was simply lost, no trace ever found, leaving his end one of the early mysteries of Pacific exploration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-gar:
Francisco Garcia de la Rosa Figueroa, born late in the eighteenth century at Toluca in the Archdiocese of Mexico. He was a Franciscan administrator of extraordinary powers who directed his order's affairs in New Spain for more than forty years.

His great service to history came in 1790, when a royal order required copying all documents on New Spain's history for Spain. Viceroy Revillagigedo entrusted him with selecting, arranging, and copying them. In less than three years he delivered thirty-two folio volumes of almost a thousand pages each, in duplicate, drawn from convent archives and private collections. They cover the civil and church history of Mexico, New Mexico, Texas, Coahuila, and the Pacific coast, a treasure for later historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-genoa:
Genoa, an archdiocese in Liguria on Italy's northwest coast, grew from a storm-sheltered harbor into the Mediterranean's greatest trading city. Its bay, guarded by Portofino's promontory and two piers, drew Carthaginian sack in 205 BC for siding with Rome, then Lombard and Saracen raids in 641, 935, and 1008. Trade still rose until Genoa rivaled Pisa.

The town became a commune under consuls in 1052, then a republic of doges from 1339 to 1797. Its fleet carried crusaders east, won Syrian ports and trading rights, and took Almeria and Tortosa from the Moors in 1147. Innocent II rewarded Genoese help against a schism with Sardinia and Corsica. Barbarossa confirmed its liberties, and it stayed imperial in sympathy until Frederick II's day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-goa:
Goa is the East Indies patriarchate, first among the sees of the Portuguese dominions in the East. Its archbishop, residing at Panjim, or New Goa, holds the honorary rank of Primate of the East and, since 1886, Patriarch of the East Indies. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a see whose suffragans stretch from India to China and East Africa.

The province takes in Mozambique in East Africa, Macao in China, and Cochin, Mylapore, and Damão in India. Its patronage belongs to the Crown of Portugal. Portuguese conquest in India began with Vasco da Gama's arrival in 1498, and missionaries of many orders built churches along the coast. A see created in 1534 became an independent archbishopric in 1557, adding Macao in 1576, Funai in Japan in 1588, and sees at Peking and Nanking in 1690.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-genoa:
John of Genoa, often called Balbi, was a Dominican grammarian whose Catholicon served as a Latin textbook for over a century. Born at Genoa, date unknown, he gave his wealth to the city's poor and entered the Dominicans at an advanced age, dying about 1298. Nothing is known of his early life and education.

His Summa Grammaticalis, commonly the Catholicon, covers orthography, etymology, grammar, prosody, rhetoric, and an etymological dictionary of Latin at every level. Its many manuscripts and numerous editions in the first seventy-five years of printing attest its wide acceptance. Erasmus attacked it caustically, Leander Alberti defended it, and the entry judges that, given the author's materials and the age's needs, the work possessed considerable merit. He also wrote a theological dialogue and a work on movable feasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miguel-cabell:
Miguel Cabello de Balboa, a secular priest born at Archidona in Spain, emigrated to Peru in 1566, his dates of birth and death unknown. From Peru he went to Quito in Ecuador, where he began his Miscelanea Antartica, finishing it at Lima in 1586. The work ranges over South American history and antiquities, drawing on native traditions and early colonial sources.

Nothing else is known of him except that in 1602-1603 he wrote a letter. It gives valuable details on the regions of Pelechuco and Apolobamba in eastern Bolivia, between the Andes and the Beni River. Though he does not explicitly say he visited those districts, the information implies it. The letter survives from a book by Father Cabello of which nothing else is known, and the Miscelanea remains his chief monument.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modesto-lafue:
Modesto Lafuente y Zamalloa, Spanish critic and historian, was born at Ravanal de los Caballeros on 1 May 1806 and died at Madrid on 25 October 1866. He received his early education in his native town, then took courses at the universities of Santiago, Astorga, and Valladolid, receiving a Bachelor of Theology degree at Valladolid in 1832.

He was appointed to the philosophy chair and later to the theology chair at the University of Astorga, but stayed only a short time, deciding to devote himself to journalism. Moving to Madrid, he published with success a critical and satirical newspaper titled Fray Gerundio. His great work, a multi-volume general history of Spain, made him his country's most popular historian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samoa:
Samoa, also called the Navigators' Islands, lies between 13 and 14 degrees south and 168 and 173 degrees west. Its fertile volcanic and coral islands are led by Savai'i, Upolu, Tutuila, and Manu'a. Its people, tall and hardy seafarers once fierce in war, lived under an aristocratic federation of chiefs drawn from certain families. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces missions among a debating, courteous people.

John Williams of the London Missionary Society began Protestant work in 1830, and in 1836 Gregory XVI split Oceania between the Sacred Hearts fathers and the Marists. Marist priests landed in 1845, and in 1851 the vicar apostolic of Central Oceania also became administrator of Samoa, a double charge held by Bishops Elloy and his successors. The entry gives the islands' geography and government before its church story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sinaloa:
The diocese of Sinaloa in Mexico, suffragan to Durango, covers the state of Sinaloa, 27,552 square miles, with 323,499 people in 1910. Culiacan, the state capital and bishop's residence, counted 13,578. The territory was discovered in 1530 by Nuño de Guzman, ill-reputed founder of San Miguel de Culiacan. A few Spaniards settled there, but Guzman's cruelties brought a terrible insurrection, until Tapia's humane measures restored confidence.

Though colonized from the early 1500s, most of the land outside a few strong places stayed in fierce pagan tribes' hands, for whose conversion Jesuits labored early in the 1600s. After subduing and evangelizing the Piaxtla mission and handing its settlements to Durango's bishop, they spread over the northern state, administering Chinipas and Sinaloa missions fruitfully until their expulsion by Charles III. In 1891 Sinaloa became a suffragan of the new Durango archdiocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-catherine-:
St. Catherine of Genoa, Caterina Fieschi Adorno, was born at Genoa in 1447 and died at the same place on 15 September 1510. This entry follows a life better described as a state than as a life in the ordinary sense. At about twenty-six she became the subject of one of the most extraordinary workings of God in a soul on record. The result was a marvellous inward condition that lasted till her death.

In that state she received wonderful revelations. She spoke of them at times to those around her, but they are mainly embodied in the Dialogues of the Soul and Body and the Treatise on Purgatory, two celebrated works. Modern biographies of her mostly translate or adapt an old Italian one, mingling outward facts with accounts of her supernatural state and doctrine. That old life rested on memoirs by her own confessor and a friend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vasco-nunez-d:
Vasco Núñez de Balboa found the Pacific Ocean from Central America's west coast. Born in Spain in 1475, either at Badajoz or Jerez de los Caballeros, he died at Darien in 1517. He reached Central America in 1500 with Rodrigo de Bastidas and later slipped away in secret with Martín Fernández de Enciso to Cartagena. The tale that he boarded hidden in a barrel or wrapped in a sail may be true.

He soon took a leading role in the expedition and founded Darien in 1509, then proclaimed himself governor and sent Enciso and Nicuesa away. From Darien he crossed the isthmus with a few followers and on 25 September 1513 reached the Pacific, proving America's continental breadth. The entry follows his fall, when Pedrarias Dávila, named governor in 1514, had him tried and beheaded.
discoveries-in-australia-volume-1-with-a:
Survey work on the Australian coast fills John Lort Stokes's first volume, printed in London by T. and W. Boone in 1846. Stokes, a commander in the Royal Navy, inscribes it to Captain Robert FitzRoy, his old shipmate. The voyage of H.M.S. Beagle ran from 1837 to 1843, by order of the Admiralty.

Thanks at the front name Captain Beaufort for charts, and Sir John Richardson, J. E. Gray, and John Gould for natural history help. Chapters run from Plymouth to Bahia, the Cape, Swan River, and Roebuck Bay. The first sight of Port Phillip, past Shortlands Bluff into calm water, fills one bright passage. This volume holds the southern and western coasts; the tale of Owen Stanley's visits to the Arafura Sea islands stands in the title.
doe-osti-3000493-an-experimental-and-com:
Bryan Wong of the University of California, Riverside, wrote this final report for award DE-FE0032207 on algae that eat a factory's exhaust. Cellulosic ethanol plants ferment plant fibre into fuel and release nearly pure carbon dioxide as a side stream. The project fed that gas to Nannochloropsis salina, a saltwater alga that turns carbon into useful goods: lipids for biodiesel, and microcrystalline cellulose, a high-value material for films and fillers.

Cultures were tuned on real fermentation effluent gas, and the harvest was measured for cellulose output and total carbon uptake. Quantum calculations predicted how efficiently the algae convert the gas, checking the bench numbers from first principles. A life-cycle and techno-economic analysis then priced the whole integration. All milestones were completed, with a closeout meeting held in September. Two students and a postdoctoral researcher trained across both the experiments and the computing.
doe-osti-3001269-strain-to-failure-measu:
Tom Stockman, Peter Beck, Tyler Dabney and co workers measure how far chromium coatings stretch before cracking in LA-UR-25-30782, issued 30 October 2025. Chromium coated zirconium cladding is a leading accident tolerant fuel design: the coating resists the runaway oxidation that wrecked fuel at Fukushima. But a coating that cracks early under strain loses its protection, so strain to failure is the number designers need. Six coating variants on Zircaloy-4, made at the University of Wisconsin, were ring pull tested at room temperature.

Digital image correlation watched local strain while cameras tracked the coating itself. A high throughput pipeline, built with artificial intelligence tools, processed the flood of images. Heat treatment mattered: hotter treatments, 600 degrees for a day or 1000 degrees for an hour, raised the average strain the coatings survived. A new hoop direction test method for high temperatures was also developed for the next round.
nasa-tm-19660009042-effects-of-momentum-:
Robert G Ragsdale at Lewis Research Center studied two unlike fluids flowing together in one stream, in a paper for a June 1965 propulsion meeting in Colorado. The streams run side by side, one inside the other, which is what coaxial means. Between them lies a momentum buffer region, a zone where the fast and slow streams trade push and pull.

How that zone behaves decides how the streams mix downstream. Mixing controls burning in engines that use such flows. Ragsdale examines the buffer region's effects on the combined stream. Propulsion designers needed that picture to shape injectors and chambers that burn fuel fully, without hot spots or waste.
nasa-tm-19680009233-dynamic-characterist:
Raymond L. E. Fischer and Darryl J. Droba, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, tested a speed governor for a space generator. The machine is a ten-kilowatt Brayton cycle turboalternator. Its speed is held by a parasitic load, an electrical dummy that soaks up spare power.

The controller wakes when the output frequency climbs above its rating. It then dumps more power into the dummy load as frequency rises, braking the machine. Fischer and Droba measured the behavior in transients and off-design running. System speed stayed within a few percent, they found. That held through voltage swings and sudden load steps.
podcast-joerogan-VnL7XWH8uoA:
A former pharmaceutical sales rep tells Rogan, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, how OxyContin took over America. The insider account covers the years when the drug was pushed hard on doctors as safe and rare in abuse. The speaker watched the machine from inside.

He describes the sales tactics, the bonuses, and the way doubts were brushed aside as addiction spread. Rogan asks when the reps knew what they were selling. The segment is a grim piece of the opioid story, valuable because it comes from the sales floor rather than from a courtroom or a headline.
the-food-of-the-gods-a-popular-account-o:
Brandon Head wrote The Food of the Gods as a plain account of cocoa, taking his title from the Greek words for it, printed at London in 1903. Five chapters cover the bean from plant to cup.

Head starts with what cocoa is, then takes up its growth and care, its making into food and drink, and its long history. A last chapter sorts its sources and kinds. Extra parts treat old ways of making cocoa and the early cocoa houses of London. A color plate of East Indian workers on a Trinidad cacao estate faces the title, tying the sweet drink to hard field labor.
the-long-white-cloud-ao-tea-roa: William Pember Reeves, Agent-General in London for New Zealand, wrote The Long White Cloud: Ao Tea Roa, dated 1899. Only the title page and a note of acknowledgment are present here, so the book's chapters themselves do not appear. The note thanks Major-General Robley for a tail-piece giving a correct pattern of Maori moko, or face-tattooing. It lists photographs lent by many hands. They include views of Mount Egmont, the Te Reinga waterfall, and a New Zealand settler's home. The frontispiece is that waterfall near Gisborne.
